subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Bao sat on the edge of the pool in Melbourne, lips pale, knees knocking together. His whole body shook. The lesson had ended with a jump into the deep end, and he had gone last. Lucia, his swimming teacher, wrapped a big towel round his shoulders and sat beside him on the wet tiles. “Cold, or was the jump scary?” Bao's teeth chattered. “Both.” “Want me to rub your back to warm you up?” He nodded, and she rubbed through the towel until the shaking slowed. “You jumped anyway,” she said. He leaned against her arm.

qa.q: What did Lucia wrap round Bao's shoulders?
qa.a: Lucia wrapped a big towel round his shoulders.

qa.q: What might Bao's shaking have meant?
qa.a: It could have been cold from the pool or fear after the deep-end jump; he said both, so he was probably chilly and still a little frightened.

qa.q: Why did Lucia's response work for either cause?
qa.a: A warm towel and calm closeness help with cold and with fear, and she asked Bao, and asked before touching, instead of guessing.

qa.q: How might another child in the class read Bao's shaking?
qa.a: They might think he was only cold, not knowing the jump had scared him too.

grounding: Shows a young child's shaking that could come from cold or fear, and warmth with calm closeness easing both.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: Backstage at the school's annual day, Asif stood in his paper-crown costume, hands trembling so hard the cardboard rattled. Seema Ma'am knelt in front of him. “Your hands are shaking. Are you scared, or cold, or excited?” Asif bounced on his toes. “Excited! My Abbu is in the third row!” She smiled. “Can I hold them for a moment?” He nodded, and she held his hands, warm between hers. “Big breath with me. In… out.” The shaking eased a little. When the music began, he marched out grinning, crown still wobbling.

qa.q: Where was Asif's Abbu sitting?
qa.a: His Abbu was in the third row.

qa.q: What was Asif feeling as his hands trembled?
qa.a: He felt excited, bouncing on his toes about his Abbu watching; some nerves could be mixed in, since the shaking only eased a little.

qa.q: What did Seema do instead of assuming Asif was afraid?
qa.a: She asked whether it was fear, cold or excitement, then used warm hands and a shared breath, which help whatever the cause.

qa.q: What would change if Seema had told Asif not to be scared?
qa.a: Asif might feel misunderstood, since he was mostly excited, and could start to wonder whether he should be scared.

grounding: Shows a young child trembling from excitement that could be mistaken for fear or cold, and calm, warm closeness settling it.

subtopic: Visible reactions with multiple possible causes
passage: I'm Aditi. Last night my little brother Varun stayed up late building a block tower on the rug. His hands began to shake so much the top blocks kept falling. He wasn't crying, and the room wasn't cold. Mumma picked him up and he flopped onto her shoulder like a sack. “Too tired,” she said, tucking a blanket round him and humming. The shaking stopped once he was asleep. Next morning she told Papa, “If his hands shake like that again when he's rested, we'll ask the doctor.” I don't know what Varun felt. He just looked wobbly.

qa.q: Why did the top blocks keep falling?
qa.a: Varun's hands began to shake so much that the top blocks kept falling.

qa.q: What does Varun flopping onto Mumma's shoulder suggest about how he felt?
qa.a: It suggests he felt worn out and sleepy rather than scared, since he wasn't crying and the room wasn't cold.

qa.q: What plan did Mumma make, and why is it sensible?
qa.a: She will ask the doctor if the shaking comes again when he's rested, because shaking that keeps happening is for a doctor to check.

qa.q: How does Aditi make sense of the shaking?
qa.a: Aditi only sees the falling blocks and the flop onto Mumma's shoulder, and doesn't claim to know what Varun felt.

grounding: Shows a young child's shaking from tiredness, calm closeness settling it, and a plan to see a doctor if it keeps happening.

passage: Pankaj stubbed his toe on the doorstep of the kasba house and threw himself on the floor. “Aaaaah! My leg is broken! I'm dying!” Between wails he peeked through his fingers to see who was watching. Dilnaz Aunty, sorting rice by the window, came over without hurrying. She looked at the toe and turned it gently. “A little red. That hurt, na?” “It hurt SO much.” “A big hurt for a small bump. Want a cold spoon on it?” Pankaj considered. The wail dropped to a sniff. “A small spoon,” he said.

qa.q: What was Dilnaz doing before she came over?
qa.a: Dilnaz Aunty was sorting rice by the window.

qa.q: Why might Pankaj have peeked through his fingers while wailing?
qa.a: He likely wanted to see if anyone was watching, so the wail may have been partly about attention, though the stubbed toe still stung and he felt hurt.

qa.q: How did Dilnaz help Pankaj match his reaction to the bump?
qa.a: She checked the toe calmly, agreed it hurt and offered a small fix, which showed him a small bump needs a small response.

qa.q: What would change if Dilnaz had rushed over shouting?
qa.a: Pankaj might believe the bump really was huge and wail louder next time to get the same rush.

grounding: Shows a young child wailing theatrically over a small bump, partly for attention, and a calm adult response teaching proportion.

passage: When Esther handed Bao the bubble wand in the London park, he shrieked so loudly that pigeons burst off the path. “YES! BEST DAY OF MY WHOLE LIFE!” He spun in circles, arms flapping, and nearly knocked over a pram. Esther, his childminder, waited until he slowed. “That's a huge happy,” she said, smiling. “Can you show me a quieter happy? Like this?” She did a little hop and a grin. Bao copied her, giggling, then blew a long string of bubbles and watched them drift.

qa.q: What did Esther hand Bao?
qa.a: Esther handed Bao the bubble wand.

qa.q: What was Bao feeling when he shrieked and spun?
qa.a: He felt thrilled, but the size of the display suggests his big feelings had run ahead of his control; he may also have wanted Esther to see how much he loved it.

qa.q: Why did Esther wait before speaking?
qa.a: Waiting till he slowed let her speak calmly, and naming a huge happy before showing a quieter one taught proportion without spoiling his joy 🙂

qa.q: How might the parent with the pram see Bao's spinning?
qa.a: They might feel alarmed and annoyed at nearly being knocked over, not knowing it was all about a bubble wand.

grounding: Shows a young child squealing with over-large delight, and a calm adult response teaching proportion.

passage: Zeenat burst into the school sick room holding one finger in the air, wailing. “Blood! Blood! I need an ambulance!” A tiny red line ran along her fingertip from a paper edge. Parul, the school nurse, didn't jump up. She patted the bed. “Let's look. Show me with your fingers how big the hurt is. One is tiny, five is huge.” Zeenat held up five, then glanced at the cut and changed it to two. Parul washed it and pressed on a plaster. “A two-finger hurt, and a two-finger plaster.” Zeenat giggled and wiped her nose.

qa.q: What made the red line on Zeenat's fingertip?
qa.a: A paper edge made the tiny red line on her fingertip.

qa.q: What does Zeenat changing five fingers to two suggest?
qa.a: It suggests her first alarm was bigger than the hurt; once calmer, she felt less scared and could see the cut was small.

qa.q: How did Parul's finger scale help?
qa.a: It asked Zeenat to rate the hurt herself, which helped her match her feelings to the size of the cut.

qa.q: What is it like for Parul when children arrive wailing?
qa.a: Parul has to stay calm and check each one, since a loud wail doesn't always mean a big injury, but sometimes might.

grounding: Shows a young child wailing theatrically over a small cut, and a calm nurse helping her find a response in proportion.

passage: Note for the staff room, Monday. Thomas, Nursery B. During tidy-up I told Mahima to “pull your socks up” because she was slow. She stopped, bent down and carefully pulled up both socks, then looked at me, waiting. A few children laughed. Mahima's eyes filled. She had done exactly what I said. I knelt and told her, “You're right, you did it. I used a grown-up saying. I meant: please tidy faster.” She nodded and picked up the blocks. Note to self and team: at this age, say what we mean in plain words.

qa.q: What did Mahima do when told to pull her socks up?
qa.a: She bent down and carefully pulled up both socks.

qa.q: Why did Mahima's eyes fill when the children laughed?
qa.a: She probably felt confused and embarrassed, because she had done exactly what she was told and could not see what was funny.

qa.q: What did Thomas do to repair the mix-up?
qa.a: Thomas admitted using a grown-up saying and restated it in plain words, so Mahima knew what was meant and felt right, not silly.

qa.q: How did the laughing children see Mahima's socks?
qa.a: They saw a funny mistake, perhaps because they already knew the saying, without seeing that Mahima had listened carefully.

grounding: Shows a young child taking a saying at face value, and a teacher switching to plain, direct words.

passage: Elizabeth Chechi had to run to the well. “Rafiq, keep an eye on the goat, okay?” When she came back with the pot, Rafiq was crouched nose to nose with the goat, one eye squeezed shut, the other wide open and nearly touching its fur. Behind him, the goat was munching her marigolds. “Rafiq!” He jumped up, puzzled and hurt. “I kept my eye on it! Like you said!” Elizabeth set the pot down and laughed, then stopped. “You did. My mistake. I should have said: watch the goat and don't let it eat the flowers.”

qa.q: What was the goat eating?
qa.a: The goat was munching Elizabeth's marigolds.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when Elizabeth shouted his name?
qa.a: He felt puzzled and hurt, because he believed he had done exactly as told by keeping his eye on the goat.

qa.q: What lesson did Elizabeth take about talking to Rafiq?
qa.a: That plain, direct words work best for him, like saying watch the goat and don't let it eat the flowers.

qa.q: What is it like for Elizabeth to come back and see the marigolds?
qa.a: She is annoyed at first, but seeing Rafiq's hurt face she realises her own words caused the mix-up.

grounding: Shows a young child taking the words keep an eye on literally, and an adult realising plain language is clearest.

passage: Rain hammered the windows of the flat in Manchester. Rosa, the neighbour, came in shaking her umbrella. “Goodness, it's raining cats and dogs out there!” Tariq ran to the window and pressed his hands on the glass, searching the street. “Where? I can't see any!” He checked the sky, the bins, the bus stop. His lip began to wobble. “Are they hurt?” Rosa knelt beside him. “Oh, no cats, no dogs. It's a funny way of saying it's raining very hard.” Tariq frowned. “Then say raining very hard.” “Fair enough,” said Rosa.

qa.q: Where did Tariq look for the animals?
qa.a: Tariq checked the sky, the bins and the bus stop.

qa.q: Why did Tariq's lip begin to wobble?
qa.a: He felt worried that real cats and dogs were out in the storm and might be hurt, because he took Rosa's words at face value.

qa.q: What would help Tariq most when adults use sayings like this?
qa.a: Saying the plain meaning, or explaining the saying straight away, so he isn't left searching for animals.

qa.q: If you were Rosa, what would you want to remember?
qa.a: That young children hear words exactly, so a plain sentence like raining very hard is clearest.

grounding: Shows a young child taking an idiom about rain literally, and why plain, direct words suit this age.

passage: The doorbell rang: guests, early. Vandana hurried through the hall and stopped. A purple crayon sun covered the wall beside the shoe rack, and Abhinav stood under it, crayon still in his fist. He laughed, a high, wobbly laugh, and could not stop. “You think this is funny?” she began, then saw his other hand twisting his T-shirt hem and his eyes darting to the door. She crouched and lowered her voice. “I'm not going to shout. We'll wipe it after the guests leave, together.” The laugh stopped. Abhinav nodded hard and dropped the crayon into her hand.

qa.q: What had Abhinav drawn on the wall?
qa.a: Abhinav had drawn a purple crayon sun.

qa.q: What did Abhinav's high, wobbly laugh most likely show?
qa.a: It most likely showed nervous discomfort at being caught, not amusement; the twisting T-shirt and darting eyes point to fear of trouble.

qa.q: What made Vandana's second response work even with guests arriving?
qa.a: She noticed his worried body cues, lowered her voice and gave a clear plan for later, so he felt safe enough to stop laughing and hand over the crayon.

qa.q: How might the guests at the door have read things if Vandana had shouted?
qa.a: They might hear a scolding and a laughing child and think he was being cheeky, missing that he was scared.

grounding: Shows a preschooler laughing nervously when caught doing something wrong, and an adult's kind tone helping him feel safe.

passage: At the colony birthday party, Shalini said “pasghetti” instead of spaghetti, and three older kids burst out laughing. “Pasghetti! Say it again!” Shalini laughed too, loudly, hands over her mouth, then laughed some more while her cheeks went blotchy. She edged towards the gate. Her cousin Aparna, carrying juice cups, watched her. Shalini's laugh didn't reach her eyes. Aparna set the cups down, took her hand and walked her to the swings. “That wasn't really funny for you, was it?” she said softly. Shalini shook her head and leaned against her.

qa.q: What word did Shalini say instead of spaghetti?
qa.a: Shalini said “pasghetti”.

qa.q: Why did Shalini laugh along with the older kids?
qa.a: She probably felt embarrassed and wanted to hide it, since her cheeks went blotchy and she edged away; laughing may have seemed safer than crying.

qa.q: How did Aparna make Shalini feel safe?
qa.a: She took her away from the teasing and spoke softly, naming that it wasn't funny for her, which let Shalini show her real feeling.

qa.q: What would change if Aparna had laughed too?
qa.a: Shalini might feel even more alone and ashamed, and would likely keep masking her hurt with laughter.

grounding: Shows a preschooler laughing along while being teased, the laugh hiding discomfort, and a kind tone helping her feel safe.

passage: “Farida, what's in your mouth?” Farida's cheeks bulged. She shook her head, then giggled, crumbs falling out. “Were you in the ladoo tin?” More giggles, louder, her shoulders up near her ears. “I asked a question. Why are you laughing?” Farida laughed again and looked at the floor. Deepika took a breath and sat on the kitchen step so they were level. “Hey. You're not in big trouble. I think that's a scared laugh. Is it?” Farida nodded, eyes wet. “I took two.” “Thank you for telling me. Two is plenty before dinner, okay?” “Okay, Mumma.”

qa.q: How many ladoos did Farida say she took?
qa.a: Farida said she took two.

qa.q: What was Farida feeling when she kept giggling?
qa.a: She was most likely scared of being in trouble, shown by her raised shoulders and eyes on the floor, not amused.

qa.q: What did Deepika change that helped Farida tell the truth?
qa.a: She sat down to Farida's level, said she wasn't in big trouble and named the scared laugh, which made it safe to answer.

qa.q: Why might Deepika at first think Farida was being cheeky?
qa.a: Laughing while being asked a question can look like making fun, so at first the giggles seemed like cheek rather than fear.

grounding: Shows a preschooler giggling nervously when caught, the laugh showing discomfort, and a parent's kind tone making it safe to talk.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage: “I made karela specially, Gargi. Your favourite, na?” Nirmala Nani beamed across the table. Gargi took a bite. Her jaw stopped for a second. Then she swallowed and smiled. “Mm. Very… crispy, Nani.” “Take more!” “I'm quite full from school.” On the drive home, Mummy glanced at her. “You hate karela.” “I didn't want Nani to feel bad. She stood in the kitchen for ages.” “That was kind. You don't have to eat things you hate every time, though. You can say, ‘Just a little, Nani.’” Gargi thought about it. “Next time.” “And if something really bothers you, you tell me. Deal?” “Deal.”

qa.q: What did Nirmala Nani make for Gargi?
qa.a: Nirmala Nani made karela.

qa.q: Why did Gargi smile after her jaw stopped?
qa.a: She disliked the karela but felt affection for Nani and didn't want to hurt her after all that cooking, so she hid the grimace.

qa.q: What middle way did Mummy offer Gargi?
qa.a: She suggested asking for just a little, and reminded Gargi to tell her if something really bothers her.

qa.q: How might Nani feel if she ever learned Gargi hates karela?
qa.a: She might feel a bit embarrassed but also touched that Gargi protected her feelings.

grounding: Shows a child swallowing a grimace at disliked food to spare a grandparent's feelings, and a parent keeping the door open for real worries.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage: I'm Yash, and last month Ayesha from my class gave me a birthday present she had knitted herself: a bright orange cap, very scratchy. When I pulled it on, my forehead itched like mad. I felt my face start to scrunch, so I pushed my mouth into a smile and said, “Wow, you made this?” Ayesha said it took her three weeks. I wore it for the whole party, even though my ears burned. That night I told my dad the truth, and he laughed and said it was a kind sort of pretending. Now I wear it over a softer cap on cold mornings.

qa.q: How long did Ayesha say the cap took her?
qa.a: Ayesha said it took her three weeks.

qa.q: How did Yash feel when the cap first went on?
qa.a: Yash felt itchy and uncomfortable but also grateful and worried about hurting Ayesha, so the grimace turned into a smile.

qa.q: Why was telling Dad the truth later a wise step?
qa.a: It let Yash be honest with a trusted adult while still protecting Ayesha's feelings, so the polite face didn't hide anything that mattered.

qa.q: What would Ayesha have felt if Yash had grimaced openly?
qa.a: Ayesha might have felt hurt and embarrassed after three weeks of knitting.

grounding: Shows a child hiding a grimace at an unwanted gift to avoid hurting the giver, while staying honest with a trusted adult.

subtype: Hiding a grimace to be polite [Regulating]
passage: Class 4 notebook, Friday. Vandana, class teacher. Uday is the most polite child I teach. When the school lunch was burnt dal today, he smiled and said, “It's good, ma'am.” That's a fine social skill. But this week he also smiled after falling hard on the steps, knee bleeding, and after Rehan took his seat again. His jaw was tight each time. I don't want to break his manners; I want him to know he can drop them with me. At home time I sat with him and said, “You don't have to look fine with me. What's been hard this week?” He was quiet, then told me about the seat. I spoke to Rehan's group before the buses left.

qa.q: What did Uday say about the burnt dal?
qa.a: Uday smiled and said, “It's good, ma'am.”

qa.q: What might Uday's tight jaw behind the smiles suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he was hurt or upset underneath, hiding pain and frustration behind politeness; he may also simply have been trying hard to be good.

qa.q: How did Vandana respect Uday's manners while checking on him?
qa.a: She valued his politeness but sat with him privately, told him he didn't have to look fine with her and asked what had been hard.

qa.q: How might Uday see school differently after Vandana's question?
qa.a: He might feel safer, knowing at least one adult notices when a smile covers something and will act on it the same day.

grounding: Shows a child's polite hiding of a grimace as a social skill, and a teacher gently noticing when it also hides real distress.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: Ivan's shot went wide of the goal, and as he trudged back across the Prague schoolyard he saw Tomas, arms folded, one corner of his mouth pulled up. Heat rushed into Ivan's face. So Tomas thinks I'm useless. He almost said something sharp. Then he noticed Tomas was next in line, bouncing on his heels, picking at his sleeve. When Tomas's own shot hit the post, the same crooked smirk appeared, aimed at no one. At the water tap Ivan asked, “Were you laughing at my miss?” Tomas looked startled. “What? No. My face does that when I'm nervous.”

qa.q: Where did Tomas's own shot land?
qa.a: Tomas's shot hit the post.

qa.q: What was Ivan feeling when he first saw the smirk?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and angry, thinking Tomas saw him as useless; the heat in his face shows the sting.

qa.q: What helped Ivan avoid an unfair quarrel?
qa.a: He watched more context, noticing Tomas's nerves and the same smirk after his own miss, and then asked directly.

qa.q: How might Tomas feel on hearing he looked like he was laughing?
qa.a: Tomas might feel surprised and a bit embarrassed that his nervous face was read as mockery.

grounding: Shows a child reading a classmate's smirk as mockery, then watching the context and asking, and finding it was nervousness.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: In the school hall on science-fair day, Tushar's volcano gave one sad fizz and stopped. Across the table, Sabina's upper lip curled and she glanced at her own model. Tushar's ears went hot. Of course. She thinks hers is miles better. He wanted to say something mean. Instead he waited. When the judge reached Sabina, her hands shook so much she spilled the baking soda. After the judge moved on, Tushar muttered, “You made a face at mine.” Sabina winced. “Sorry. I was thinking, if yours fizzled, mine will too.”

qa.q: What happened when the judge reached Sabina?
qa.a: Her hands shook so much she spilled the baking soda.

qa.q: Why did Tushar's ears go hot?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and stung, reading Sabina's curled lip as her thinking her model was much better.

qa.q: What went right because Tushar waited?
qa.a: He saw Sabina's shaking hands and then asked, which showed her face came from worry, not scorn, and stopped him saying something mean.

qa.q: What was the science fair like for Sabina?
qa.a: She was nervous that her model would fail too, and her face was about her own fear rather than judging Tushar.

grounding: Shows a child reading a sneer as superiority, then seeing more context and asking, and learning it came from nerves.

subtype: Smirk and sneer as social judgement [Interpreting]
passage: I'm Rafiq, and I sit behind Samir in Class 5. On Monday the new boy, Kenji, smirked when Samir read his poem aloud. Samir's neck went red. At break he told me, “Did you see? He thinks my poem's rubbish.” I didn't know. I'd seen Kenji smirk at the fan and the blackboard too. Samir didn't shout, though. He watched Kenji for two days. On Wednesday he asked him straight out, at the tap. I couldn't hear the answer, but Samir came back shrugging. “He says he smiles like that when he's lost.” Now they share a bench.

qa.q: In which class does Rafiq sit behind Samir?
qa.a: Rafiq sits behind Samir in Class 5.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling when his neck went red?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed and hurt, believing Kenji thought his poem was rubbish.

qa.q: Which of Samir's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: Watching for two days and then asking Kenji directly worked, because it showed the smirk came from feeling lost, not from mockery.

qa.q: How does Rafiq read Kenji's smirk?
qa.a: Rafiq isn't sure, having seen Kenji smirk at the fan and the blackboard too, so the look seemed less aimed at Samir.

grounding: Shows a child reading a new classmate's smirk as mockery, then watching and asking instead of assuming an insult.

passage: The photographer had ten minutes for the whole family group, and he was shouting. “Everyone, big smile! You, the boy in blue, teeth!” Pankaj had met most of these relatives only that morning. He pressed his lips together into a small, polite curve and looked at his shoes. “Bigger! Come on!” The curve got smaller. Lakshmi Maasi, standing behind him, rested a hand lightly on his shoulder. “He's smiling his way,” she told the photographer. “Take it.” The flash went off. Later, in the printed picture, Pankaj's small smile was the one that looked real.

qa.q: How long did the photographer have for the family group?
qa.a: The photographer had ten minutes for the whole family group.

qa.q: What does Pankaj's small, closed-mouth smile suggest?
qa.a: It suggests he felt shy among relatives he had only just met and wanted to be polite; he may also have been uncomfortable with the shouting.

qa.q: How did Lakshmi Maasi support Pankaj under the time pressure?
qa.a: She calmly told the photographer to take his natural smile, so he wasn't forced into a bigger one.

qa.q: How did the photographer see Pankaj's smile?
qa.a: The photographer saw it as not enough for a good picture, missing that pushing only made the boy shrink.

grounding: Shows a child's small closed-mouth smile with new relatives carrying shyness and politeness, and an adult refusing to force a bigger one.

passage: The new family moved into the flat below theirs in Kolkata on a Sunday. When Ma sent Anirban down with a tiffin of mishti, a boy his age opened the door. “I'm Mohit.” Anirban gave a small, closed-lipped smile, held out the tiffin and said nothing. Upstairs later, Ma nearly said, “Why can't you smile properly at people?” but stopped. Anirban had always taken a while. On Wednesday, Mohit knocked with a carrom board under his arm. By the third game Anirban was laughing out loud, teeth and all, arguing about the queen.

qa.q: What did Ma send Anirban down with?
qa.a: Ma sent him down with a tiffin of mishti.

qa.q: What was Anirban feeling when he gave Mohit a small, closed-lipped smile?
qa.a: He probably felt shy meeting someone new and was being polite; it doesn't show he disliked Mohit, only that he needed time.

qa.q: Why was Ma right to stop herself?
qa.a: Anirban always takes a while, and pushing for a bigger smile could make him more self-conscious; giving time let the real smile come.

qa.q: What might Mohit have thought after the first meeting?
qa.a: Mohit might have wondered if Anirban was unfriendly, yet he still knocked on Wednesday and gave the friendship a chance.

grounding: Shows a child's small closed-mouth smile on meeting someone new, and a parent giving time instead of forcing a bigger smile.

passage: “Gurpreet, this is Imran Sir, your new maths tutor.” “Hello, Gurpreet.” Gurpreet gave a small smile, lips closed, and slid half behind her mother's chair. “Say hello properly, beta. Give a nice big smile.” The smile flickered and went. Imran pulled his chair back a little. “No rush. I was the same at your age. Shall I just start, and you tell me when I'm wrong?” He wrote 7 + 8 = 16 on the page. Gurpreet leaned forward. “That's fifteen.” “Is it? Oh no.” This time her smile had a gap in it, a missing front tooth showing.

qa.q: What sum did Imran write on the page?
qa.a: Imran wrote 7 + 8 = 16 on the page.

qa.q: Why did Gurpreet's smile flicker and go when her mother asked for a big one?
qa.a: She likely felt shy and more self-conscious when pushed, since a forced smile can feel like being watched.

qa.q: What did Imran try instead of pushing?
qa.a: He gave her space, said he had been shy too, and made a small mistake for her to fix, letting her join in her own way.

qa.q: How might Gurpreet's mother feel seeing the gap-toothed smile?
qa.a: She might feel relieved and see that time and a gentle start work better than asking for a big smile.

grounding: Shows a child's closed-mouth smile with a new adult carrying shyness, and time and gentleness bringing a real smile.

passage: Sit, Simran. You're new at this school, so let me tell you about my first year teaching. A boy in Class 3 spilled ink across the register. I scolded him, and he smiled. A wide, fixed smile. I, Nikita, twenty-two and proud, decided he was mocking me and sent him out of the room. He stood in the corridor smiling and shaking. At home time his mother said quietly, “He smiles like that when he's frightened. He always has.” I felt sick. The next morning I knelt and said sorry to him. After that, whenever a child smiled at a scolding, I lowered my voice first.

qa.q: What did the boy spill across the register?
qa.a: He spilled ink across the register.

qa.q: What was the boy feeling while he stood in the corridor smiling?
qa.a: He was frightened, as his shaking and his mother's words show; the smile was a nervous way to cope, not mockery.

qa.q: What choice did Nikita make the next morning, and why did it matter?
qa.a: She knelt and said sorry to the boy, which began to repair his trust and changed how she handled every scolding afterwards.

qa.q: How might the boy's mother have felt at home time?
qa.a: She was probably worried and sad that her frightened son had been punished for a smile she knew so well.

grounding: Shows a child's nervous smile during a telling-off being misread as cheek, and a teacher learning it signalled fear.

passage: It was raining hard, and Nilesh had just spent twenty minutes chasing their dog down the lane because Trisha had left the gate open. He came in soaked. “How many times have I told you?” Trisha stood by the door, and a smile spread over her face, tight at the edges. “You think this is funny?” he snapped. The smile got wider, and her eyes filled. Nilesh stopped, dripping on the mat. Her hands were twisted together at her chest. He had seen that face before, the day she broke the vase. He took a towel, sat down and said more quietly, “I'm cold and cross. You're not in huge trouble. The latch, from now on, okay?” The smile finally dropped, and she nodded, crying a little.

qa.q: How long had Nilesh spent chasing the dog?
qa.a: Nilesh had spent twenty minutes chasing their dog down the lane.

qa.q: What did Trisha's widening smile and filling eyes show?
qa.a: They showed she felt scared and ashamed and was trying to calm her angry father, not that she found it funny.

qa.q: What made Nilesh's second response better than the first?
qa.a: He noticed her twisted hands, remembered her earlier nervous smile, sat down and spoke quietly, so she could drop the smile.

qa.q: What would change if Nilesh had kept reading the smile as cheek?
qa.a: He might have punished a frightened child, and Trisha could learn to hide her fear even more.

grounding: Shows a child smiling nervously while being told off, and a tired parent noticing the fear before treating it as cheek.

passage: The cricket ball had cracked the society secretary's scooter mirror, and now he stood over Zubin in the Pune parking lot, voice booming. “Do you know what this costs?” Zubin's mouth pulled into a small, fixed smile. “Oh, you're smiling? You think it's a joke?” Zubin's smile trembled but wouldn't go. Afreen, from the third floor, had been watching from the stairs. She came down. “Uncle, look at his hands,” she said quietly. Zubin's fingers were clenched white around the bat. The secretary looked. His voice dropped. “All right. Tell your parents tonight, and we'll sort out the mirror.” Zubin nodded, still smiling, eyes wet.

qa.q: What had the cricket ball cracked?
qa.a: It had cracked the society secretary's scooter mirror.

qa.q: Why might Zubin keep smiling while being shouted at?
qa.a: He was probably frightened and embarrassed, and the smile may have been a way to calm the angry secretary, as his white-clenched fingers suggest.

qa.q: How did Afreen help the secretary read Zubin correctly?
qa.a: She quietly pointed to his clenched hands, giving evidence that the smile came from fear rather than cheek.

qa.q: How might the secretary feel after looking at Zubin's hands?
qa.a: The secretary might feel a little ashamed of shouting and see a scared boy instead of a cheeky one.

grounding: Shows a child's appeasing smile while being told off, and a bystander helping an adult see fear instead of cheek.

passage: Xin and Priscila were partners for fractions in their Sydney classroom. Priscila suggested cutting the pizza drawing into eighths. Xin went silent, brows pulled down hard, pencil tapping. Priscila's stomach sank. She's annoyed with me. I said something silly. She scooted her chair a little away and stopped talking. After a minute Xin looked up. “Eighths works! I was checking if sixths would too.” Priscila blinked. “You looked so cross.” Xin laughed. “That's my thinking face. My brother says I look like I want to fight the page.” “Maybe warn me next time?” “Deal. I'll say ‘thinking’.”

qa.q: What did Priscila suggest cutting the pizza drawing into?
qa.a: Priscila suggested cutting it into eighths.

qa.q: What was Priscila feeling when Xin's brows pulled down?
qa.a: She felt anxious and embarrassed, believing Xin was annoyed at her suggestion, so she moved away and went quiet.

qa.q: What small step did the girls agree on?
qa.a: Xin would say “thinking” when frowning over work, so Priscila wouldn't mistake the face for anger 👍

qa.q: How does Xin see her own frown?
qa.a: Xin sees it as a normal thinking face, even joking about it, and hadn't realised it looked cross to others.

grounding: Shows a child's furrowed brow over maths being misread by a partner as anger, and a simple explanation preventing friction.

passage: Study hour in the hostel common room was silent except for the ceiling fan. Bidisha leaned across to borrow Imran's ruler. He looked up with his forehead deeply creased, eyebrows almost meeting, and said nothing. Bidisha pulled her hand back fast. What did I do? For the rest of the hour she didn't look at him. At dinner the warden, who had seen it, sat beside her. “You know Imran makes that face over every long division? Last week he frowned at one sum for ten minutes and then cheered.” Bidisha glanced over. Imran was frowning at his dal, too.

qa.q: What did Bidisha lean across to borrow?
qa.a: Bidisha leaned across to borrow Imran's ruler.

qa.q: Why did Bidisha pull her hand back fast?
qa.a: She felt hurt and worried, reading Imran's creased forehead as anger at her for interrupting.

qa.q: How did the warden help clear up the misunderstanding?
qa.a: The warden quietly explained that Imran frowns like that when working hard, giving Bidisha another reading of the face.

qa.q: How might Imran feel if he knew Bidisha had avoided him all hour?
qa.a: Imran might feel surprised and sorry, since his frown was about long division, not about her.

grounding: Shows a child's furrowed brow over schoolwork being misread by a peer as anger, and an explanation that it means thinking.

passage: I'm Pradeep, and I sit between Chaitanya and Neel in maths. On Tuesday, during the word problems, Chaitanya scowled so hard his eyebrows made a V. He was staring past me towards Neel's side. Neel whispered, “Why's he glaring? What's his problem?” and started muttering back. I don't know what goes on inside Chaitanya's head, but I've seen that V over every sum since Class 2. So I leaned over to Neel. “He's not angry. That's how he thinks. Watch.” A minute later Chaitanya's face cleared, he scribbled, and he grinned at nobody. Neel snorted and went back to his sheet.

qa.q: What shape did Chaitanya's eyebrows make?
qa.a: His eyebrows made a V.

qa.q: What was Neel feeling when he whispered about the glare?
qa.a: Neel felt annoyed and a bit defensive, thinking Chaitanya was glaring at him.

qa.q: How did Pradeep prevent a quarrel?
qa.a: Pradeep explained that the frown was Chaitanya's thinking face and told Neel to watch, which gave him another reading before things got worse.

qa.q: How might Chaitanya react if he learned Neel thought he was glaring?
qa.a: Chaitanya would probably be surprised, since he was only focused on the word problem.

grounding: Shows a child's furrowed brow over maths being misread by a classmate as anger, and an explanation that it means thinking.

passage: Dolma slid her notebook onto the pile, the last one in, with a brown stain across the cover. Kalyani Ma'am picked it up and raised one eyebrow. Dolma's stomach dropped. She's angry. She thinks I'm careless. She wanted to run back to her seat. Instead she remembered her Pala saying a question deserves an answer. “The roof leaked on my table last night,” she said. “I dried it by the stove. The pages are all there.” Kalyani Ma'am's eyebrow came down. She flipped through. “So they are. Thank you for telling me. Next time a plastic cover, maybe?”

qa.q: What was across the cover of Dolma's notebook?
qa.a: A brown stain was across the cover.

qa.q: What was Dolma feeling when Kalyani Ma'am raised one eyebrow?
qa.a: She felt scared and ashamed, thinking the teacher was angry and saw her as careless.

qa.q: Why did explaining work better than running back to her seat?
qa.a: Treating the eyebrow as a question gave Kalyani Ma'am the real reason, the leaking roof, and turned doubt into understanding.

qa.q: What did the raised eyebrow probably mean to Kalyani Ma'am?
qa.a: It likely meant a simple question about the stain, not anger, since she thanked Dolma once she heard the reason.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's raised eyebrow as anger, then treating it as a question and explaining, which works better.

passage: I'm Nazia, and I was next in line for the class presentations. Arnab was showing his poster on the water cycle when Sir raised one eyebrow at the arrow from the clouds back to the sea. Arnab stopped. His voice went sharp. “It's right! I checked!” The class went still. Sir's eyebrow stayed up. “I didn't say it was wrong. I'm asking why it goes that way.” Arnab's ears turned pink. He looked at his poster, then explained that rain falls into the sea too. Sir nodded slowly. “Good. Add a label.” I can't know what Arnab felt, but he sat down very fast.

qa.q: What was Arnab's poster about?
qa.a: Arnab's poster was on the water cycle.

qa.q: Why did Arnab's voice go sharp when Sir raised an eyebrow?
qa.a: He probably felt defensive and embarrassed, reading the eyebrow as a sign Sir thought he was wrong.

qa.q: What could Arnab try next time a teacher raises an eyebrow?
qa.a: He could treat it as a question and simply explain his thinking, as he did in the end, instead of defending himself first.

qa.q: How did Nazia see the moment?
qa.a: Nazia saw the class go still and Arnab sit down fast, but doesn't claim to know what Arnab felt.

grounding: Shows a child reading a teacher's raised eyebrow as disapproval, and how explaining in answer to the question works better.

passage: Monday: Bhupen said the answer to 6 × 7 was 48. Sarita Ma'am raised one eyebrow. Bhupen went red and didn't speak for the rest of the lesson, sure she was cross. Wednesday: At home he told his Dada about it. Dada raised one eyebrow at him, slowly. “What am I saying now?” Bhupen squinted. “Are you asking something?” “I'm asking, ‘Are you sure?’ That's all.” Friday: Bhupen wrote 54 for 6 × 9, and up went Sarita Ma'am's eyebrow. His heart thumped, but he looked again. “I checked. 6 × 9 is 54.” She nodded. “Good. You checked.”

qa.q: What did Bhupen say 6 × 7 was on Monday?
qa.a: Bhupen said the answer to 6 × 7 was 48.

qa.q: What was Bhupen feeling when the eyebrow went up on Friday?
qa.a: He felt nervous, his heart thumping, but more confident than on Monday because he now read the eyebrow as a question.

qa.q: What did Dada teach Bhupen, and how did it help?
qa.a: Dada showed that a raised eyebrow can simply ask “Are you sure?”, so on Friday Bhupen checked and explained instead of going silent.

qa.q: What would Sarita Ma'am have wanted on Monday when she raised her eyebrow?
qa.a: She probably wanted Bhupen to check his answer, not to feel scolded, and his silence may have puzzled her.

grounding: Shows a child learning over several days to read a teacher's raised eyebrow as a question rather than anger.
